deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivations. It continues Hilbert's notes on university mathematics teaching. The next page (numbered 101) supplies the outline's header: 'Beim Universitätsunterricht stehen 3 Punkte im Vordergrund: 1.) Anknüpfung an die Schulkenntnisse ... a. Differential- und Integralrechnung' (in university teaching three points are paramount: 1.) connection to school knowledge, a. differential and integral calculus). This page appears to continue that outline, although it is physically folio 100.

The page sets out the following:

(1b) Algebra, from which three branches lead: elimination theory, invariant theory and algebraic number fields (Zahlkörper).

(1c) Geometry: its axioms, topology, and 'higher geometry'.

(2) Training of future (Gymnasium) teachers: particular emphasis on b (algebra) and c (geometry).

(3) Preserving the scientific standpoint. Especially in the first lectures, everything should be done exactly. All assumptions, e.g. those of the continuum, should be stated explicitly as axioms. The ultimate ('letzten') axioms of the science are those about calculating with the rational integers. One need not, and cannot, go back that far in every lecture. But one must say where one starts; that is what is scientific.

Position (3) is a programmatic statement. Analysis rests on explicitly stated continuum axioms, and those in turn ultimately rest on the arithmetic of the integers. This is in the spirit of the arithmetization of analysis (Weierstrass, Dedekind, Kronecker). It anticipates Hilbert's later axiomatic treatment of the real numbers ('Über den Zahlbegriff', 1900), where completeness/continuity is an explicit axiom.

The surrounding pages give some context for dating. They mention the Franco-Prussian war analogy and learning from Hurwitz and Minkowski. This suggests Hilbert's Königsberg period or early Göttingen period, probably the 1890s; this dating is my inference.

results.usually_credited_to: Common in the period (Kronecker, Gordan, Dedekind traditions); Hilbert's own research areas in the 1880s-90s

results.what: Geometry curriculum including its axioms and topology
results.modern_name: Axiomatic foundations of geometry; analysis situs/topology
results.usually_credited_to: Pasch (1882), Hilbert (Grundlagen der Geometrie, 1899); 'Topologie' as a term from Listing (1847)

results.what: Pedagogical principle: state continuum assumptions explicitly as axioms; the ultimate axioms are those of integer arithmetic; always say where one starts
results.usually_credited_to: Weierstrass, Dedekind, Kronecker (arithmetization); Hilbert (axiomatic method, 'Über den Zahlbegriff' 1900)

deep.surprise_reason: These are pedagogical and programmatic remarks fully consistent with Hilbert's known views on the axiomatic method and on teaching. The early explicit insistence on continuum axioms grounded in integer arithmetic is a pleasant documentary detail of his developing axiomatic outlook, but it is not new mathematics.
